lessonTitle: Common Presentations in Primary Care: Cough, Fatigue, Back Pain and Skin Problems

blocks.text: A man in his sixties says his 'smoker's cough' has been the same for years. But for three weeks it has sounded different, and this morning he saw a streak of blood. In primary care, a presenting symptom is almost always benign, but occasionally it is the first sign of something serious; the skill is to tell which, and to decide what to do next.

blocks.markdown: **A framework for common presentations.** Most consultations for cough, fatigue, back pain and skin problems end in reassurance, simple treatment or watchful waiting, because the pre-test probability of serious disease is low in the community. A safe approach has four steps. **(1)** Take a focused history: duration, trajectory, associated symptoms, risk factors (smoking, occupation, family history, medicines) and the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations. **(2)** Examine proportionately. **(3)** Look actively for *red flags*. **(4)** Choose one of three actions: **treat** now, **observe** (watchful waiting with a defined review), or **refer** (routine, urgent or emergency), and always give safety-netting advice.

blocks.title: Red flag
blocks.text: A red flag is a symptom, sign or risk factor that raises the probability of serious pathology (such as cancer, infection, fracture or neurological compromise) enough to change management: for example by prompting an investigation or referral. A red flag is a prompt to think, not a diagnosis; most patients with one have a benign cause, and a patient with no red flags still needs safety-netting.

blocks.markdown: **Persistent cough.** Most acute coughs are self-limiting viral illness. A cough persisting beyond about three weeks needs more thought. Ask about smoking, haemoptysis, weight loss, breathlessness, chest pain, night sweats, occupational exposures (for example asbestos), medicines (ACE inhibitors can cause a dry cough), reflux, post-nasal drip and asthma symptoms. Examine the chest, check for finger clubbing and lymph nodes, and consider a chest X-ray. National suspected-cancer guidance (NICE NG12) sets out when to request an urgent chest X-ray or make an urgent referral: check the current guidance for the exact age and symptom criteria, because it is updated. Smoking exposure is quantified in *pack-years*.

blocks.caption: One pack-year is 20 cigarettes (one pack) per day for one year.

blocks.title: Quantifying smoking in a patient with a persistent cough
blocks.prompt: A 52-year-old woman has had a dry cough for 5 weeks. She has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years. State her pack-years and how this changes your approach.

steps.text: A pack contains 20 cigarettes, so 20 per day equals one pack a day.

Interpret: a significant smoking history, together with a persistent cough, raises the pre-test probability of lung disease (including lung cancer and COPD), so you would examine her, ask about other red flags and follow current NICE suspected-cancer guidance for imaging.
Offer stop-smoking support now and safety-net: return urgently for haemoptysis, breathlessness or weight loss, whatever the chest X-ray shows.

blocks.answer: 25 pack-years, which lowers the threshold for investigation and requires a structured follow-up.

blocks.markdown: **Fatigue.** Tiredness is common and usually multifactorial: sleep, mood, life stress, anaemia, thyroid disease, diabetes, medicines, alcohol, post-viral states, and occasionally malignancy or chronic infection. The history should cover onset, sleep pattern, mood, weight change, bowel and urinary symptoms, fever, night sweats and drug and alcohol use. A limited, targeted set of tests is reasonable (for example full blood count, ferritin, thyroid function, glucose or HbA1c, kidney and liver function, inflammatory markers and urinalysis), guided by the history; check current local and NICE guidance and avoid reflex 'screening' of everything. Unintentional weight loss is a key red flag, and the percentage lost is more informative than the kilograms.

blocks.caption: $W$ is body weight in kg. Unintentional loss of about 5% or more over 6 to 12 months is commonly regarded as clinically significant; thresholds vary by guideline.

blocks.title: Is the weight loss significant?
blocks.prompt: A 56-year-old man reports six months of tiredness. His weight was 92 kg a year ago and is 85 kg today; he has not been dieting. Calculate his percentage weight loss and explain your next step.

steps.text: Divide by the starting weight and multiply by 100.

A loss of about 7.6% unintentionally over a year exceeds the commonly used 5% marker for significance, so he needs a more thorough assessment: full examination including lymph nodes and abdomen, targeted blood tests, and consideration of the relevant urgent suspected-cancer pathway (check current guidance).
Document the finding, share the reasoning with him, and book a short, defined review rather than leaving the outcome open.

blocks.answer: About 7.6% unintentional weight loss: a red flag in a patient with fatigue, prompting urgent targeted work-up.

blocks.markdown: **Back pain.** Most low back pain is non-specific (mechanical) and improves within weeks. The task is to exclude the small group with serious pathology. Ask about age at onset (under 20 or over 50 to 55), previous cancer, fever, night or rest pain, weight loss, trauma, osteoporosis or steroid use, intravenous drug use or immunosuppression, and neurological symptoms. **Cauda equina syndrome** (compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots) is a surgical emergency: ask about saddle numbness, new bladder or bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction and bilateral or progressive leg weakness. Current NICE guidance (NG59) discourages routine imaging for non-specific low back pain and emphasises staying active, self-management and appropriate analgesia chosen with the BNF.

rows: Persistent cough
Haemoptysis, weight loss, age over 40 with smoking, clubbing, hoarseness
Lung cancer, TB, other lung disease
Urgent chest X-ray or suspected-cancer referral per current NICE guidance
Fatigue
Unintentional weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, fever, bleeding
Malignancy, haematological disease, chronic infection
Targeted tests, examine fully, urgent referral if suspicious
Low back pain
Saddle numbness, new urinary retention or incontinence, bilateral leg weakness
Cauda equina syndrome
Same-day emergency assessment
Low back pain
Age under 20 or over 55, previous cancer, night pain, fever
Cancer, infection, fracture
Urgent assessment and imaging or referral depending on features
Pigmented skin lesion
Change in size, shape or colour, irregular border, bleeding
Melanoma
Urgent suspected skin cancer referral; do not biopsy in primary care unless local protocol says so
blocks.caption: Red-flag lists are teaching summaries; check the current NICE, SIGN and local referral guidance for the exact criteria and timescales.

blocks.title: Treat, observe or refer?
blocks.prompt: A 34-year-old man has had 4 days of low back pain after moving furniture. He has no leg symptoms, no bowel or bladder change, no fever and no history of cancer. He is neurologically normal. Decide what to do.

steps.text: Screen for red flags systematically: age, trauma, fever, cancer history, night pain, neurological and sphincter symptoms. None are present, so the probability of serious pathology is very low.
Examine proportionately: inspect gait and spine, check lumbar movement, straight leg raise, power, sensation and reflexes in the legs.
Choose observation with treatment: explain the good prognosis, advise staying active and returning to normal activity, and offer simple analgesia chosen with the current BNF and NICE guidance.

Safety-net explicitly: seek urgent care for numbness in the saddle area, difficulty passing or controlling urine or stool, new leg weakness or fever, and offer a review if no improvement within a defined period.

blocks.answer: Observe and treat conservatively, with explicit safety-netting. No imaging is needed for non-specific low back pain without red flags.

blocks.markdown: **Skin problems.** Most skin consultations concern eczema, acne, fungal infections and benign lesions. The key red flag is a changing pigmented lesion. The ABCDE rule (asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter, evolution) and the NICE seven-point checklist support recognition of melanoma. A suspected melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma is referred urgently on a suspected-cancer pathway; check the current timescales. Always examine the whole skin when assessing one lesion, and use a dermatoscope only if trained to do so.

blocks.title: Safety-netting is part of the treatment
blocks.text: Whichever action you choose (treat, observe or refer), tell the patient what to expect, what would make things worse, and exactly when and how to seek help. Record that you did so. Omitting this is how serious disease is missed in the 'no red flags' group.

points: Use a four-step framework for common presentations: focused history, proportionate examination, search for red flags, then treat, observe or refer with safety-netting.
Persistent cough, unintentional weight loss, new neurological or sphincter symptoms in back pain, and a changing pigmented lesion are red flags needing action under current NICE guidance.
Quantify risk: pack-years for smoking and percentage weight loss for fatigue make the history objective.
Most low back pain without red flags is managed by reassurance, activity and analgesia chosen with the BNF; cauda equina syndrome is a same-day emergency.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had a cough for four weeks. She is otherwise well. Which is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Request a CT scan of the head
Reassure her that no assessment is needed because most coughs are viral
Take a focused history including smoking, red flags and medicines, then examine her chest and decide on further investigation
Prescribe an antibiotic and review in three months

questions.correctOptionText: Take a focused history including smoking, red flags and medicines, then examine her chest and decide on further investigation

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: a head CT has no role in a cough assessment.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a cough beyond about three weeks warrants assessment, not automatic reassurance.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a persistent cough needs a structured assessment before deciding whether to treat, observe or investigate.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: antibiotics are not indicated empirically and a three-month gap is unsafe.

questions.explanation: A cough lasting several weeks is no longer a typical self-limiting viral illness, so the first step is a careful history (smoking, haemoptysis, weight loss, medicines such as ACE inhibitors) and examination. Investigations and referral follow from the findings and current NICE guidance.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with 3 days of low back pain. She also reports numbness around her genitals, and has twice failed to pass urine this morning. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Arrange same-day emergency assessment for suspected cauda equina syndrome
Prescribe simple analgesia and review in two weeks
Advise rest and a hot water bottle and review at the next routine appointment

questions.correctOptionText: Arrange same-day emergency assessment for suspected cauda equina syndrome

distractorRationale.a: Correct: saddle numbness with urinary retention suggests cauda equina syndrome, which needs emergency assessment.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this delays a time-critical emergency.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: rest and routine follow-up would risk permanent neurological damage.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: physiotherapy is for non-specific pain and routine referral is far too slow.

questions.explanation: Saddle anaesthesia and bladder dysfunction in a patient with back pain indicate possible compression of the cauda equina, where delay increases the risk of permanent loss of bladder, bowel and sexual function. This is why these features are classic red flags that mandate same-day emergency assessment.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman treated for breast cancer five years ago reports 6 weeks of thoracic and lumbar back pain that wakes her at night and is not eased by rest. Neurological examination is normal. Which management is most appropriate?

options.text: Urgent assessment for possible spinal metastases, following current NICE and local pathways, with safety-netting for neurological symptoms
Strict bed rest and review in three months
Reassurance and advice to stay active, as most back pain is mechanical

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent assessment for possible spinal metastases, following current NICE and local pathways, with safety-netting for neurological symptoms

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prior cancer with unrelenting night pain should prompt urgent assessment for metastatic disease.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: physiotherapy alone does not exclude serious pathology.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: bed rest is not recommended and the delay is unsafe.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: previous cancer and night pain are red flags that make mechanical pain a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.explanation: A history of cancer, persistent night pain and pain unrelieved by rest raise the pre-test probability of bony metastasis above the very low baseline in non-specific back pain. Urgent assessment is therefore appropriate even with a normal neurological examination. Check the current NICE guidance for the exact route and timescale.

questions.stem: In a patient presenting with fatigue, a broad panel of blood tests should be ordered routinely in every case before taking a history.
questions.explanation: The history guides which tests are useful, and indiscriminate testing generates incidental abnormal results with little diagnostic yield. A targeted set of tests, chosen according to symptoms, risk factors and current guidance, is more effective and safer.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man notices a pigmented mole on his back has grown over three months, has an irregular border and has bled twice. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat with a topical steroid and review in six months
Reassure him because most moles are benign
Remove it in the surgery and do not send it for histology
Urgent referral on the suspected skin cancer pathway (check the current timescale), with safety-netting

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent referral on the suspected skin cancer pathway (check the current timescale), with safety-netting

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: a topical steroid is not a treatment for a suspicious pigmented lesion.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: changing size, irregular border and bleeding are red flags for melanoma.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: an excision without histology is unsafe and not appropriate.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the features suggest possible melanoma and need urgent suspected-cancer referral.

questions.explanation: Evolution (growth), irregular border and bleeding are features of melanoma on the ABCDE and seven-point checklists, so the lesion should be referred urgently for specialist assessment. Check the current NICE suspected-cancer guidance for the exact referral route and timescale.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has a persistent cough. He has smoked 30 cigarettes per day for 22 years. Using 20 cigarettes as one pack, calculate his smoking exposure in pack-years.
questions.explanation: Thirty cigarettes per day equals 30/20 = 1.5 packs per day. Multiplying by 22 years gives 1.5 x 22 = 33 pack-years, which is a significant exposure and lowers the threshold for investigating a persistent cough.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman attends with fatigue and loss of appetite. She weighed 80 kg six months ago and weighs 74 kg today, unintentionally. What is her percentage weight loss?
questions.explanation: The loss is 80 - 74 = 6 kg. Dividing by the starting weight gives 6/80 = 0.075, or 7.5%. A loss above about 5% unintentionally over 6 to 12 months is generally regarded as significant, so this is a red flag requiring a thorough work-up.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with 3 months of tiredness. Outline how you would assess her in primary care and how you would decide between treating, observing and referring.
markingGuide: Focused history: onset and pattern, sleep, mood and stressors, diet, alcohol and medicines, bleeding, weight change, fever or night sweats, symptoms of thyroid disease or diabetes
Her ideas, concerns and expectations (for example fear of cancer)
Examination including pallor, lymph nodes, thyroid, abdomen, cardiovascular and mental state
Targeted investigations guided by the history (for example full blood count, ferritin, thyroid function, glucose, kidney and liver function, inflammatory markers); check current guidance
Red flags (unintentional weight loss, lymphadenopathy, night sweats, fever) leading to urgent referral
If no red flags: treat identified causes, address sleep and mood, and observe with a defined review date
Safety-netting advice
questions.explanation: Fatigue is usually multifactorial, so a structured history and examination, followed by limited targeted tests, is more productive than broad testing. The choice between treat, observe and refer depends on red flags and on findings, and is always accompanied by safety-netting.

questions.stem: Discuss how you would triage a patient presenting with back pain into emergency, urgent and routine management. Include examples of the features that place a patient in each group.
markingGuide: Emergency: suspected cauda equina syndrome (saddle numbness, new bladder or bowel dysfunction, bilateral or progressive leg weakness); same-day assessment

Urgent: suspected cancer (previous malignancy, weight loss, night pain, age over 55), infection (fever, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression) or fracture (trauma, osteoporosis, steroids); urgent investigation or referral
Routine or self-managed: non-specific low back pain without red flags; reassurance, activity, analgesia chosen with the current BNF and NICE guidance
Importance of a neurological examination of the legs
Explicit safety-netting for all groups, with a defined review date
Avoid routine imaging for non-specific pain
questions.explanation: A good answer matches clinical features to urgency categories and explains why: the cost of missing cauda equina or infection is high, while most pain is benign and self-limiting. The answer must also mention safety-netting for those managed conservatively.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old non-smoking man has had a dry cough for five weeks after a cold. His chest examination is normal, he has no weight loss, haemoptysis or breathlessness, and he is on no regular medicines. Justify whether you would observe, treat or refer, and describe your safety-netting.
markingGuide: Features favour a post-viral cough with low pre-test probability of serious disease
No red flags: age, non-smoker, no weight loss, haemoptysis or abnormal examination
Reasonable option is observation with a defined review (for example in a few weeks), possibly with a chest X-ray if concern persists; check current NICE guidance
Explain that post-viral cough can last several weeks and antibiotics are not helpful
Consider other causes if it persists: asthma, reflux, post-nasal drip
Safety-net: return for haemoptysis, breathlessness, weight loss, fever or if cough persists beyond the agreed review date
Record the discussion
questions.explanation: The patient has a low probability of serious disease, so watchful waiting with a clear review point is appropriate. The safety net protects against the rare patient who proves to have something more serious.
